cases.title: formatFloat keeps trailing zeros in the integer part
cases.notes: Only the FRACTION is trimmed. A blanket trailing-zero strip turns 1200 into 12.

cases.title: formatFloat expands 1e300 exactly, never exponentially
cases.notes: The severe one. toFixed goes exponential at 1e21, and a trailing-zero strip then eats the EXPONENT: (1e300).toFixed(14) is '1e+300', which strips to '1e+3'. 1e300 was written into spreadsheets as 1e3 — not a crash, not invalid XML, just a different number in a file someone opens later and believes. NOTE the golden is NOT 1 followed by 300 zeros: number_format prints the exact value of the double, and the nearest double to 1e300 is not 10^300.

cases.title: formatFloat does not go exponential at the 1e21 boundary
cases.notes: 1e21 is exactly where JS toFixed switches notation. `<v>1e+21</v>` is not valid cell content, so a reader may reject the whole sheet.

cases.title: formatFloat collapses negative zero to 0
cases.notes: Both engines already agreed here — this was listed as a divergence in the polyglot plan and checking proved it was not one. Kept because both sides drop the sign INCIDENTALLY (via number_format / toFixed) rather than by decision, so a faster hand-rolled formatter would reintroduce it.

cases.title: formatFloat keeps 14 decimal places
cases.notes: 14, not 15 or 17. The step where two implementations pick different precision is invisible until someone diffs two documents.

cases.title: formatFloat keeps the sign on a real negative
numericStringToNumber reads exponent notation
cases.notes: parseInt stops at the first non-digit, so '1e5' became 1. PHP has read exponent notation in numeric strings since PHP 7, and the JS helper's own docstring claimed it mirrored PHP.

cases.title: numericStringToNumber reads a negative exponent
cases.notes: PHP's dot-test-then-(int) path returned 0 for this — a value silently becoming zero is the worst failure mode in the table.

cases.title: numericStringToNumber does not clamp at the platform integer max
cases.notes: PHP's (int) '1e21' clamps to PHP_INT_MAX (9223372036854775807), which is not the number anyone wrote. Rust and Go have the same trap with i64.

cases.title: numericStringToNumber ignores leading zeros
cases.notes: Must NOT be read as octal — a trap in several languages' parse routines.

cases.title: roundMoney rounds a positive half away from zero
cases.notes: PHP round() and JS Math.round() agree here, which is exactly why the divergence below went unnoticed.

cases.title: roundMoney rounds a negative half away from zero
cases.notes: LIVE DIVERGENCE at the time this suite was written. PHP round(-2.5) is -3 (half away from zero); JS Math.round(-2.5) is -2 (half toward +Infinity). fancy-mlm-js's amountAsInt is documented as a mirror of fancy-mlm-php's and is not one. Reachable through configuration: levelFactors is `.map(Number)` off host config with no sign validation, so a negative factor produces a negative reward, and the two backends then pay different amounts for the same event.

cases.title: roundMoney rounds -0.5 to -1, not to zero
cases.notes: The starkest row: JS Math.round(-0.5) is -0, so a clawback of half a unit becomes NOTHING on one backend and a whole unit on the other.

cases.title: roundMoney is symmetric about zero
cases.notes: The property that matters for money: |round(-x)| == |round(x)|. A credit and its matching clawback must cancel exactly, or a ledger drifts by a unit per reversal.

cases.title: roundMoney rounds below a half toward zero
cases.notes: Both engines already agree. Present so an implementation switching to a blanket floor/ceil fails rather than passing the halves by luck.

cases.title: roundMoney rounds above a half away from zero
